l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 22
s: Mencius describes Bo Yi and Tai Gong seeking king Wen because they heard that the chief of the West knew how to nourish the old. He explains that a prince who nourished the old would attract all men of virtue, and that this required regulating fields and dwellings, planting mulberry trees, raising animals, and instructing families. Under king Wen, the people had silk and flesh for the old, while farms secured families against want, so no aged people were starved or famished.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 22
s: Mencius explains why Bo Yi and Tai Gong sought king Wen and describes what it means for a ruler to nourish the old.

l: Bo Yi, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 22
s: Bo Yi was dwelling on the coast of the northern sea to avoid Zhou. On hearing of the rise of king Wen, he decided to go and follow him because he had heard that the chief of the West knew well how to nourish the old.

l: king Wen, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 22
s: King Wen is presented as the chief of the West who knew well how to nourish the old. Among his people, agricultural and household regulations ensured that the aged had warmth and food.

l: Tai Gong Wang, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 22
s: Tai Gong was dwelling on the coast of the eastern sea to avoid Zhou. On hearing of the rise of king Wen, he decided to go and follow him because he had heard that the chief of the West knew well how to nourish the old.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 22
s: A prince in the kingdom who knew well how to nourish the old would become the proper object for all men of virtue to gather to.

l: a prince (the kingdom's hypothetical prince), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 22
s: A prince who nourished the old would attract all men of virtue. He would do so by regulating fields and dwellings, teaching the planting of mulberry trees and the raising of animals, and instructing families to nourish their aged.

l: old people, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 22
s: Old people were to receive silk for clothing and flesh for food. At fifty, silk was needed to maintain warmth, and at seventy, flesh was necessary to satisfy the appetite.

l: all men of virtue, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 22
s: All men of virtue would feel that a prince who knew well how to nourish the old was the proper object for them to gather to.

l: each family, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 22
s: Each family had five brood hens and two brood sows, kept to their breeding seasons, so that the old could have flesh to eat.

l: the people of king Wen, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 22
s: The people of king Wen had no aged people who were starved or famished.

l: food, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 22
s: Food for the old came from families raising brood hens and brood sows, while the cultivation of 100-mu farms secured families of eight mouths against want.

l: the rise of king Wen, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 22
s: The rise of king Wen prompted Bo Yi and Tai Gong to decide to follow him after they heard that the chief of the West knew well how to nourish the old.

l: nourishing the old, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 22
s: Nourishing the old involved regulating fields and dwellings, planting mulberry trees, raising animals, and instructing wives and children to care for their aged. It provided the old with silk to wear and flesh to eat.

l: starvation and famine, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 22
s: Persons who were not kept warm or supplied with food were described as starved and famished. Among the people of king Wen, no aged people suffered this condition.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 23
s: Mencius explains how a sage should govern the kingdom to make the people prosperous and virtuous. He recommends well-cultivated fields, light taxes, seasonal use of food resources, and spending wealth only on prescribed ceremonies. He compares abundant grain and pulse to water and fire, which people readily share. He concludes that when grain and pulse are abundant, the people will be virtuous.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 23
s: Mencius says that fields should be well cultivated, taxes should be light, food resources should be used seasonably, and wealth should be spent only on prescribed ceremonies. He teaches that a sage should govern so that pulse and grain become as abundant as water and fire.

l: the people, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 23
s: The people may become rich when their fields are well cultivated and their taxes are light. They cannot live without water and fire, and when pulse and grain are abundant, they will be virtuous.

l: grain, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 23
s: Grain should be abundant under good governance, as abundant as water and fire. Its abundance is connected with the people's virtue.

l: taxes, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 23
s: Taxes should be made light so the people may become rich.

l: food, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 23
s: The people should use their resources of food seasonably.

l: wealth, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 23
s: The people should expend their wealth only on the prescribed ceremonies. When food is used seasonably and wealth is properly spent, wealth will be more than can be consumed.

l: prescribed ceremonies, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 23
s: The prescribed ceremonies are the proper objects on which the people should expend their wealth.

l: water, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 23
s: The people cannot live without water. Water is so abundant that a person asking for it at dusk will receive it.

l: fire, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 23
s: The people cannot live without fire. Fire is so abundant that a person asking for it at dusk will receive it.

l: sage, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 23
s: A sage governs the kingdom so that pulse and grain are as abundant as water and fire.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 23
s: The kingdom should be governed so that pulse and grain become abundant and the people become virtuous.

l: virtue, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 23
s: Virtue is expected among the people when pulse and grain are as abundant as water and fire.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 24
s: Mencius explains that Confucius’s ascent of the eastern hill and the Tai mountain changed how large Lu and the world beneath heaven appeared to him. He compares this expanded perspective with the sea and the gate of the sage, after which other waters and other people’s words seem less significant. Mencius also teaches that water should be observed in waves and that flowing water advances only after filling the hollows in its course. The student who follows the doctrines of the sage progresses by completing one lesson after another.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 24
s: Mencius teaches that broader understanding changes how Lu, the world, other waters, and other people’s words appear. He also explains how to contemplate water and compares the student’s progress to flowing water filling hollows.

l: Confucius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 24
s: Confucius ascended the eastern hill, and Lu appeared small to him. He then ascended the Tai mountain, and all beneath the heavens appeared small.

l: Lu, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 24
s: Lu appeared small to Confucius after he ascended the eastern hill.

l: Tai mountain, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 24
s: Confucius ascended the Tai mountain, after which all beneath the heavens appeared small to him.

l: sea, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 24
s: A person who has contemplated the sea finds it difficult to think anything of other waters.

l: gate of the sage, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 24
s: A person who has wandered in the gate of the sage finds it difficult to think anything of the words of others.

l: sage, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 24
s: The sage is associated with a gate whose teachings make other people’s words difficult to value in comparison.

l: water, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 24
s: Water should be contemplated as foaming in waves. Flowing water does not proceed until it has filled the hollows in its course.

l: student, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 24
s: The student who has set his mind on the doctrines of the sage advances to them by completing one lesson after another.

l: the doctrines of the sages, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 24
s: The doctrines of the sage are approached by the student gradually, through completing one lesson after another.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 25
s: Mencius distinguishes between two ways of beginning the day. A person who rises at cock-crowing and earnestly practices virtue is described as a disciple of Shun. A person who rises at cock-crowing and earnestly pursues gain is described as a disciple of Zhi. Mencius says that the interval between the thought of gain and the thought of virtue separates Shun from Zhi.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 25
s: Mencius distinguishes disciples of Shun from disciples of Zhi by whether they earnestly practice virtue or pursue gain. He says that the interval between the thought of gain and the thought of virtue separates Shun from Zhi.

l: Shun, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 25
s: Shun is associated with the person who rises at cock-crowing and addresses himself earnestly to the practice of virtue.

l: Zhi, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 25
s: Zhi is associated with the person who rises at cock-crowing and addresses himself earnestly to the pursuit of gain.

l: virtue, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 25
s: Virtue is something a person may earnestly practice after rising at cock-crowing. Its thought is contrasted with the thought of gain.

l: gain, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 25
s: Gain is something a person may earnestly pursue after rising at cock-crowing. Its thought is contrasted with the thought of virtue.

l: interval between gain and virtue, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 25
s: The interval between the thought of gain and the thought of virtue separates Shun from Zhi.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 26
s: Mencius compares the principles of Yang, Mo, and Zi Mo. Yang holds that each person should act for himself, while Mo loves all equally and would make any bodily sacrifice to benefit the kingdom. Zi Mo holds a medium between them, but Mencius says that refusing to adapt it to circumstances makes it like rigidly holding one point. Mencius rejects such rigidity because it harms right principle by ignoring many other considerations.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 26
s: Mencius compares the principles of Yang, Mo, and Zi Mo. He says that Zi Mo’s medium is nearer the right but becomes harmful when held without regard for circumstances.

l: Yang, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 26
s: Yang holds that each one should act for himself. He would not pluck out a single hair even if doing so could benefit the whole kingdom.

l: Mo, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 26
s: Mo loves all equally. He would have rubbed smooth his whole body from crown to heel if that could benefit the kingdom.

l: Zi Mo, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 26
s: Zi Mo holds a medium between the principles of Yang and Mo. His position is nearer the right, but holding it rigidly without allowing for circumstances becomes like holding one point.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 26
s: The kingdom could have benefited from Yang plucking out a single hair. Mo would accept the loss of all the hair on his body if it benefited the kingdom.

l: Each one for himself, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 26
s: Each one for himself is the principle attributed to Yang. It means that each person acts for himself rather than making a personal sacrifice for the kingdom.

l: the true medium, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 26
s: The medium is the position Zi Mo holds between Yang and Mo. It is nearer the right, but without room for changing circumstances it becomes rigid and harmful.

l: right principles, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 26
s: Right principle is injured by holding to one point without regard for other circumstances. Such rigidity takes up one point and disregards a hundred others.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 27
s: Mencius explains that hunger and thirst can make people mistake any food or drink for having the right taste. He says that hunger and thirst injure the palate and also injure men's minds. A person who prevents these conditions from harming the mind need not be troubled about not being equal to other men.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 27
s: Mencius says that hunger and thirst distort people's taste and injure both the palate and men's minds. He teaches that preventing these conditions from harming the mind removes sorrow about not being equal to other men.

l: hunger, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 27
s: Hunger makes people think any food is sweet and injures the palate. It can also injure the mind.

l: thirst, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 27
s: Thirst makes people think any drink has the right taste and injures the palate. It can also injure the mind.

l: mind (men's minds), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 27
s: Men's minds can be injured by hunger and thirst. If a man prevents these conditions from harming his mind, he need not sorrow about not being equal to other men.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 28
s: Mencius says that Hui of Liu Xia would not have changed his firm purpose of life even for the three highest offices of State. The unit concerns Hui of Liu Xia’s steadfastness and his refusal to sacrifice his principles for political position.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 28
s: Mencius says that Hui of Liu Xia would not have changed his firm purpose of life even for the three highest offices of State.

l: Hui of Liu Xia, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 28
s: Hui of Liu Xia would not have changed his firm purpose of life even for the three highest offices of State.

l: firm purpose of life, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 28
s: Hui of Liu Xia would not have changed his firm purpose of life for the three highest offices of State.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 29
s: Mencius compares a man with definite aims to be accomplished to someone digging a well. He says that digging to a depth of seventy-two cubits and stopping before reaching the spring amounts to throwing away the well. The unit concerns persistence in pursuing definite aims.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 29
s: Mencius compares a man with definite aims to be accomplished to someone digging a well. He teaches that stopping before reaching the spring means the effort is ultimately wasted.

l: man with definite aims to be accomplished, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 29
s: A man with definite aims to be accomplished is compared to one digging a well. If he stops before reaching the spring, his effort is likened to throwing away the well.

l: well, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 29
s: A well is dug to a depth of seventy-two cubits but is abandoned before reaching the spring. Mencius says that stopping at that point is throwing away the well.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 30
s: Mencius says that benevolence and righteousness were natural to Yao and Shun. Tang and Wu made benevolence and righteousness their own. The five chiefs of the princes feigned them and, having borrowed them for a long time without returning them, made it difficult to know that they did not own them.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 30
s: Mencius says that benevolence and righteousness were natural to Yao and Shun, were made their own by Tang and Wu, and were feigned by the five chiefs of the princes.

l: benevolence and righteousness, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 30
s: Benevolence and righteousness were natural to Yao and Shun. Tang and Wu made them their own, while the five chiefs of the princes feigned them.

l: Yao, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 30
s: Benevolence and righteousness were natural to Yao.

l: Shun, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 30
s: Benevolence and righteousness were natural to Shun.

l: Tang, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 30
s: Tang made benevolence and righteousness his own.

l: Wu, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 30
s: Wu made benevolence and righteousness his own.

l: five chiefs of the princes, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 30
s: The five chiefs of the princes feigned benevolence and righteousness. Having borrowed them for a long time without returning them, they made it difficult to know that they did not own them.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 31
s: Gong Sun Chou asks Mencius about Yi Yin’s banishment of Tai Jia to Tong when Tai Jia was disobedient to reason. The people were pleased when Tai Jia was banished and again pleased when Yi Yin brought him back after Tai Jia became virtuous. Gong Sun Chou asks whether worthy ministers may banish sovereigns in this way when they are not virtuous. Mencius replies that they may do so only if they share Yi Yin’s purpose; otherwise, it would be usurpation.

l: Gong Sun Chou, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 31
s: Gong Sun Chou asks Mencius whether worthy ministers may banish sovereigns who are not virtuous, as Yi Yin banished Tai Jia.

l: Yi Yin, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 31
s: Yi Yin said he could not be near and see Tai Jia so disobedient to reason, and he banished Tai Jia to Tong. When Tai Jia became virtuous, Yi Yin brought him back.

l: Tai Jia, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 31
s: Tai Jia was banished to Tong by Yi Yin for being disobedient to reason. After Tai Jia became virtuous, he was brought back.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 31
s: Mencius says that worthy ministers may banish their sovereigns if they have the same purpose as Yi Yin. If they do not have that purpose, Mencius says the act would be usurpation.

l: the people, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 31
s: The people were much pleased when Tai Jia was banished to Tong and were again much pleased when he was brought back after becoming virtuous.

l: purpose, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 31
s: Mencius teaches that sharing Yi Yin’s purpose determines whether a minister’s banishment of a sovereign is permissible.

l: usurpation, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 31
s: Mencius says that banishing a sovereign without the same purpose as Yi Yin would be usurpation.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 32
s: Gong Sun Chou asks Mencius why superior men are seen eating without labouring, citing the Book of Poetry’s warning against eating the bread of idleness. Mencius explains that when a superior man lives in a country and its sovereign follows his counsels, the country gains tranquillity, wealth, and glory. He adds that when the country’s young follow the superior man’s instructions, they become filial, obedient to their elders, true-hearted, and faithful.

l: Gong Sun Chou, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 32
s: Gong Sun Chou asks Mencius why superior men appear to eat without labouring.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 32
s: Mencius explains the benefits a superior man brings to a country through his counsel and instruction.

l: superior man, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 32
s: A superior man, when residing in a country, can guide its sovereign toward tranquillity, wealth, and glory. Through his instructions, the young can become filial, obedient to their elders, true-hearted, and faithful.

l: country, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 32
s: A country gains tranquillity, wealth, and glory when its sovereign employs the counsels of a superior man. Its young become filial, obedient to their elders, true-hearted, and faithful when they follow his instructions.

l: bread of idleness, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 32
s: The bread of idleness is presented as something the Book of Poetry says a person should not eat.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 33
s: Dian asks Mencius about the business of the unemployed scholar. Mencius says that the unemployed scholar should exalt his aim by setting it simply on benevolence and righteousness. He explains that killing an innocent person is contrary to benevolence and taking what one has no right to is contrary to righteousness. He concludes that when benevolence is the heart’s dwelling and righteousness the path of life, the business of a great man is complete.

l: Dian, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 33
s: Dian asks Mencius what the business of the unemployed scholar is and asks what it means to exalt the aim.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 33
s: Mencius replies that the unemployed scholar’s business is to exalt his aim by setting it on benevolence and righteousness.

l: unemployed scholar, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 33
s: The unemployed scholar should exalt his aim by committing himself simply to benevolence and righteousness.

l: aim, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 33
s: The aim is exalted when it is set simply on benevolence and righteousness.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 33
s: Benevolence means that putting a single innocent person to death is rejected as contrary to it, and it should be the dwelling-place of the heart.

l: righteousness, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 33
s: Righteousness means that taking what one has no right to is rejected as contrary to it, and it should be the path of life.

l: great man, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 33
s: The great man has completed his business when benevolence is the dwelling-place of the heart and righteousness is the path of life.

l: business, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 33
s: The business of the unemployed scholar is to exalt his aim, while the business of a great man is complete when he lives with benevolence and righteousness.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 34
s: Mencius argues that Chen Zhong would refuse the kingdom of Qi if it were offered contrary to righteousness. People regard Chen Zhong as a man of the highest worth because he would decline a dish of rice or a plate of soup. Mencius says that disowning parents and relatives, or rejecting the relations of sovereign and minister and of superiors and inferiors, are greater crimes. He concludes that a man should not receive credit for great excellences merely because he possesses a small one.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 34
s: Mencius argues that refusing the kingdom of Qi when it is offered contrary to righteousness is only a small righteousness. He says that disowning parents and relatives and rejecting the relations of sovereign and minister, superiors and inferiors, are greater crimes.

l: kingdom of Qi, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 34
s: The kingdom of Qi is imagined as being offered to Chen Zhong contrary to righteousness. Chen Zhong would not receive it.

l: Chen Zhong, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 34
s: Chen Zhong would refuse the kingdom of Qi if it were offered contrary to righteousness. People regard him as a man of the highest worth because he would decline a dish of rice or a plate of soup.

l: righteousness, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 34
s: Righteousness is associated with declining a dish of rice or a plate of soup and with refusing the kingdom of Qi when it is offered contrary to righteousness. Mencius presents this as only a small form of righteousness compared with other moral obligations.

l: parents and relatives, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 34
s: Disowning parents and relatives is described as one of the greatest crimes a man can commit.

l: greatest crimes, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 34
s: The greatest crimes include disowning parents and relatives and rejecting the relations of sovereign and minister, superiors and inferiors.

l: relation of sovereign and minister, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 34
s: The relation of sovereign and minister is identified as an important relation that must not be rejected. Rejecting it is described as a greater crime than declining a dish of rice or a plate of soup.

l: relation of superiors and inferiors, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 34
s: The relation of superiors and inferiors is identified as an important relation that must not be rejected. Rejecting it is described as a greater crime than declining a dish of rice or a plate of soup.

l: great excellences, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 34
s: Great excellences should not be credited to a man merely because he possesses a small excellence. Mencius uses Chen Zhong's small act of righteousness to illustrate this point.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 35
s: Tao Ying asks Mencius what would happen if Gu Sou had murdered a man while Shun was sovereign and Gao Yao was chief minister of justice. Mencius says Gao Yao would apprehend Gu Sou because he had received the law from a proper source. Shun would not forbid the apprehension, but would abandon the kingdom, carry Gu Sou into concealment by the sea-coast, and live there cheerfully for the rest of his life.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 35
s: Mencius explains to Tao Ying that Gao Yao would apprehend Gu Sou if Gu Sou had murdered a man. He says Shun would not forbid this because Gao Yao had received the law from a proper source.

l: Shun, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 35
s: Shun would not prevent Gao Yao from apprehending Gu Sou. He would regard abandoning the kingdom as throwing away a worn-out sandal, carry Gu Sou into concealment along the sea-coast, and remain there cheerful and happy for life.

l: Gao Yao, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 35
s: Gao Yao, as chief minister of justice, would apprehend Gu Sou if Gu Sou had murdered a man. He had received the law from a proper source.

l: Gu Sou, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 35
s: Gu Sou is presented in a hypothetical case as having murdered a man. Shun would privately carry him into concealment and live with him along the sea-coast.

l: murder of a man, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 35
s: The hypothetical murder of a man by Gu Sou would lead Gao Yao to apprehend him.

l: law, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 35
s: The law had been received by Gao Yao from a proper source.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 35
s: Shun would abandon the kingdom as though throwing away a worn-out sandal. He would forget the kingdom while living cheerfully and happily in concealment along the sea-coast.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 36
s: Mencius, traveling from Fan to Qi, saw the king of Qi's son and reflected on how position alters a person's air and appearance. He said that the residence, carriages and horses, and dress of the king's son were mostly like those of other men, but his position made him look different. Mencius taught that position has an even greater influence in the wide house of the world. He also recounted that the prince of Lu's voice was recognized as resembling their prince's because their positions corresponded.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 36
s: Mencius went from Fan to Qi, saw the king of Qi's son at a distance, and discussed how position alters air and appearance. He also recounted the story of the prince of Lu at the Die Shi gate.

l: Qi, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 36
s: Qi was the destination of Mencius's journey from Fan. The king of Qi's son was present there.

l: king Xuan of Qi, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 36
s: The king of Qi's son looked different from other men even though his residence, carriages and horses, and dress were mostly the same as theirs. Mencius attributed this difference to his position.

l: position, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 36
s: Position alters a person's air and can make someone look different even when his residence, carriages and horses, and dress resemble those of other men. Corresponding positions also accounted for the prince of Lu's voice resembling that of their prince.

l: air, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 36
s: Air is altered by a person's position, just as nurture affects the body. A peculiar air should distinguish someone whose position is in the wide house of the world.

l: prince of Lu, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 36
s: When the prince of Lu went to Song, he called out at the Die Shi gate. The gatekeeper recognized that his voice closely resembled that of their prince because of the correspondence of their positions.

l: influence of position, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 36
s: The influence of position is described as great. It changes a person's air and appearance and can produce a similarity in voice between people holding corresponding positions.

l: Mencius's journey from Fan to Qi, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 36
s: During his journey from Fan to Qi, Mencius saw the king of Qi's son at a distance and reflected on the effect of position.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 37
s: Mencius says that feeding a scholar without loving him treats him like a pig, while loving him without respecting him keeps him like a domestic animal. He teaches that honouring and respecting come before offering gifts. A superior man cannot be retained by demonstrations of honour and respect that lack genuine reality.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 37
s: Mencius says that feeding a scholar without loving him treats him as a pig, and loving him without respecting him keeps him as a domestic animal. He teaches that honouring and respecting precede any offering of gifts.

l: scholar, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 37
s: A scholar who is fed without being loved is treated as a pig. If he is loved without being respected, he is kept as a domestic animal.

l: honouring and respecting, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 37
s: Honouring and respecting exist before any offering of gifts. When they lack genuine reality, empty demonstrations of them are insufficient.

l: superior man, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 37
s: A superior man may not be retained by empty demonstrations of honouring and respecting.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 38
s: Mencius explains that bodily organs and their functions belong to Heaven-conferred nature. He says that a man must be a sage to satisfy the design of his bodily organization. The unit concerns the relationship between bodily organization, nature, and sagehood.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 38
s: Mencius teaches that bodily organs and their functions belong to Heaven-conferred nature, and that a man must be a sage to satisfy the design of his bodily organization.

l: man (Mencius's man), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 38
s: A man must be a sage before he can satisfy the design of his bodily organization.

l: bodily organs, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 38
s: The bodily organs have functions that belong to Heaven-conferred nature.

l: Heaven-conferred nature, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 38
s: Heaven-conferred nature includes the bodily organs and their functions.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 39
s: King Xuan of Qi wanted to shorten the period of mourning. Gong Sun Chou argued that observing mourning for one whole year was better than eliminating it altogether. Mencius said that the proper response was to teach filial piety and fraternal duty, not merely suggest moderation. When the king's son could observe only a few months because of an impossibility, Mencius said that even one additional day of mourning was better than none.

l: king Xuan of Qi, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 39
s: He wanted to shorten the period of mourning.

l: Gong Sun Chou, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 39
s: He said that one whole year's mourning was better than doing away with mourning altogether. He asked Mencius about the case of the king's son.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 39
s: He said that merely urging moderation was insufficient and that the proper course was to teach filial piety and fraternal duty. He distinguished between someone prevented from completing mourning and someone who could complete it but neglected it.

l: mourning, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 39
s: Mourning for one whole year was presented as better than eliminating it. When completing the whole period was impossible, even adding a single day was considered better than not mourning at all.

l: Dian, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 39
s: His mother died, and his tutor asked that he be allowed to observe mourning for a few months. He wanted to complete the whole period but found it impossible to do so.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 40
s: Mencius identifies five ways in which the superior man effects his teaching. His influence may descend like seasonable rain, perfect virtue, develop talents, answer inquiries, or encourage private self-cultivation and correction. These five methods describe how the superior man teaches different people.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 40
s: Mencius states that the superior man effects his teaching in five ways.

l: superior man, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 40
s: The superior man teaches through timely influence, perfecting virtue, developing talents, answering inquiries, and encouraging private self-cultivation and correction.

l: teaching, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 40
s: Teaching is effected through five methods: seasonable influence, perfecting virtue, assisting talents, answering inquiries, and encouraging self-cultivation and correction.

l: five ways of teaching, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 40
s: The five ways are the superior man's influence descending like seasonable rain, perfecting virtue, assisting the development of talents, answering inquiries, and privately cultivating and correcting oneself.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 41
s: Gong Sun Chou says that Mencius's principles are lofty and admirable but difficult to attain. He asks why Mencius does not adapt his teaching to make the principles seem attainable and encourage learners to exert themselves daily. Mencius replies that a great artificer does not alter the marking-line for a stupid workman, nor did Yi change his rule for drawing the bow for a stupid archer. He says the superior man draws the bow without discharging the arrow, appears to leap with it to the mark, and stands exactly in the middle of the path for those who are able to follow him.

l: Gong Sun Chou, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 41
s: Gong Sun Chou says that Mencius's principles are lofty and admirable but may be impossible to reach. He asks why Mencius does not adapt his teaching to make the principles seem attainable and encourage learners to exert themselves daily.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 41
s: Mencius says that a great artificer does not alter or do away with the marking-line for a stupid workman, and that Yi did not change his rule for drawing the bow for a stupid archer. He explains that the superior man draws the bow without discharging the arrow, appears to leap with it to the mark, and stands exactly in the middle of the path.

l: principles, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 41
s: The principles are described by Gong Sun Chou as lofty and admirable, but difficult to attain.

l: teaching, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 41
s: Gong Sun Chou asks Mencius to adapt his teaching so that learners will consider the principles attainable and exert themselves daily.

l: superior man, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 41
s: The superior man draws the bow but does not discharge the arrow, having seemed to leap with it to the mark. He stands exactly in the middle of the path, and those who are able follow him.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 42
s: Mencius explains how a person's principles relate to the state of the kingdom. When right principles prevail throughout the kingdom, a person's principles appear together with the person. When right principles disappear, the person must vanish along with those principles. Mencius says he has not heard that one's principles depend on other men for their manifestation.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 42
s: Mencius explains that when right principles prevail throughout the kingdom, a person's principles appear along with the person. He also states that he has not heard of principles depending on other men for their manifestation.

l: right principles, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 42
s: Right principles prevail throughout the kingdom in one circumstance, in which a person's principles appear with the person. When right principles disappear from the kingdom, the person's principles and person must vanish together.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 42
s: The kingdom is described as a place where right principles may either prevail throughout or disappear.

l: person (the individual whose principles are discussed), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 42
s: The person appears along with the person's principles when right principles prevail throughout the kingdom. When right principles disappear, the person must vanish along with the person's principles.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 43
s: Gong Du asks Mencius why he did not answer Geng of Tang despite the propriety of showing consideration to him when he appeared in Mencius's school. Mencius explains that he does not answer people who presume on their nobility, talents, age, services performed for him, or old acquaintance. He says that two of these presumptions were chargeable on Geng of Tang.

l: Gong Du, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 43
s: Gong Du asks Mencius why he did not answer Geng of Tang when Geng of Tang appeared in Mencius's school.

l: Geng of Tang, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 43
s: Geng of Tang appeared in Mencius's school and was chargeable with two forms of presumption that Mencius said prevented him from answering.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 43
s: Mencius explains that he does not answer people who presume on nobility, talents, age, services performed for him, or old acquaintance. He says that two of these presumptions applied to Geng of Tang.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 44
s: Mencius teaches that stopping where one should not stop leads to stopping in everything. He says that behaving shabbily toward people who deserve good treatment leads to shabby behavior toward everyone. He also observes that advancing too quickly is followed by a rapid retreat.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 44
s: Mencius teaches that stopping where stopping is not allowable leads to stopping in everything. He also says that shabby treatment of those who deserve good treatment leads to shabby treatment of all, and that precipitate advancement is followed by a speedy retreat.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 45
s: Mencius distinguishes the superior man’s different attitudes toward inferior creatures, people generally, and his parents. The superior man is kind to inferior creatures but does not love them. He loves people generally but is not affectionate toward them, while he is affectionate to his parents. He is lovingly disposed to people generally and kind to creatures.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 45
s: Mencius states distinctions among the superior man’s attitudes toward inferior creatures, people generally, and his parents.

l: the superior man, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 45
s: The superior man is kind to inferior creatures but not loving toward them. He is loving toward people generally but not affectionate, and he is affectionate to his parents.

l: inferior creatures, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 45
s: Inferior creatures receive kindness from the superior man, but not love.

l: people generally, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 45
s: People generally receive love and a loving disposition from the superior man, but not affection.

l: parents, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 45
s: The superior man is affectionate to his parents.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 46
s: Mencius explains that the wise and the benevolent should embrace broadly while concentrating most earnestly on what is of the greatest importance. He says Yao and Shun did not know or attend to everything, but focused on what mattered most. He contrasts proper mourning and eating practices to show that people may attend to minor rules while neglecting what is most important.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 46
s: Mencius teaches that the wise should embrace all knowledge while focusing on what is of the greatest importance, and that the benevolent should embrace all in their love while cultivating earnest affection for the virtuous.

l: the wise, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 46
s: The wise embrace all knowledge, but they are most earnest about what is of the greatest importance.

l: what is of the greatest importance, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 46
s: What is of the greatest importance is the proper focus of earnest attention for the wise and the benevolent.

l: the benevolent, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 46
s: The benevolent embrace all in their love, but they focus most earnestly on cultivating affection for the virtuous.

l: the virtuous, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 46
s: The virtuous are the proper objects of the benevolent's earnest affection.

l: Yao, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 46
s: Yao's wisdom did not extend to everything, but he attended earnestly to what was important.

l: Shun, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 46
s: Shun's wisdom did not extend to everything, but he attended earnestly to what was important.

l: wisdom, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 46
s: The wisdom of Yao and Shun did not extend to everything, and it was shown through earnest attention to what was important.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 46
s: The benevolence of Yao and Shun did not show itself in acts of kindness to every man, but in earnestly cultivating affection for the virtuous.

l: the three years' mourning, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 46
s: The three years' mourning is presented as something a person may be unable to keep, while being very particular about shorter mourning periods.

l: ignorance of what is most important, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Chapter 46
s: Ignorance of what is most important is shown by failing to keep the three years' mourning or eating immoderately while inquiring about the rule against tearing meat with the teeth.

l: Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 38
s: Mencius discusses benevolent rule, the dangers of unjust war, and the importance of governing through virtue, righteousness, and proper principles. He explains how the people, the sovereign, government, and the doctrines of the sages relate to one another. He also distinguishes natural human desires and feelings from the appointment of Heaven, and describes the superior man, scholars, and sages. Confucius is presented as an example of proper conduct and as a transmitter of earlier doctrines.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 38
s: Mencius teaches that benevolence begins by extending care from what one values to what one does not initially care for. He criticizes unjust war, excessive taxation, false virtue, uncontrolled desires, and neglect of self-cultivation, while explaining the proper conduct of rulers, scholars, and the superior man.

l: Confucius, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 38
s: Confucius is described as leaving Lu gradually but leaving Qi abruptly, and as suffering because the rulers and ministers of his time did not sympathize with him. He sought scholars pursuing the true medium, and when he could not find them, turned to the ardent and the cautiously-decided; he also transmitted the doctrines of earlier sages.

l: the sovereign, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 38
s: The sovereign is considered less important than the people and the spirits of the land and grain. To become sovereign, one must gain the peasantry, and a sovereign who endangers the altars may be replaced.

l: the people, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 38
s: The people are the most important element in a nation. They suffer when rulers demand multiple forms of exaction at once, and they may welcome a ruler who performs benevolent correction.

l: scholars, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 38
s: Scholars may be laughed at when they return to acts associated with their former occupations, and they may suffer from the mouths of men. Mencius distinguishes ambitious scholars, cautiously-decided scholars, and the good careful people of the villages, whom Confucius called thieves of virtue.

l: the superior man, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 38
s: The superior man does not treat the pursuit of natural pleasures as simply his nature, nor moral conduct as merely the appointment of Heaven. He cultivates himself, follows the law of right without seeking emolument, despises the pomp of great rulers, and seeks to restore an unchanging standard.

l: a sage, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 38
s: A sage is a teacher of a hundred generations whose example can purify the corrupt, strengthen the weak, enlarge the mean, and make the niggardly liberal. The sages' doctrines are transmitted across generations, from Yao and Shun through Tang, king Wen, and Confucius.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 38
s: Benevolence is the distinguishing characteristic of man and, in conduct, is called the path of duty. Extending one's feeling of reluctance to injure others produces benevolence, and a benevolent ruler has no enemy under heaven.

l: righteousness, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 38
s: Righteousness results from extending the feeling that refuses to do certain wrongs to actions one might otherwise perform. It requires following the proper path, speaking and acting sincerely, and refusing to pursue gain by guile.

l: virtue, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 38
s: Virtue is weakened by conduct that merely resembles sincerity, purity, or disinterestedness while agreeing with corrupt customs. The doctrines of Yao and Shun and the true standard of virtue are needed to expose such appearances.

l: the appointment of Heaven, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 38
s: The appointment of Heaven is connected with natural pleasures such as tastes, colors, sounds, odors, and ease. Moral relations and conduct are also called the appointment of Heaven, though the superior man does not describe them in exactly the same way as natural desires.

l: government, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 38
s: Government and its business are among the precious things of a prince, and without their great principles there will not be enough wealth for expenditure. Proper government requires rules of propriety, distinctions of right, and the trust placed in men of virtue and ability.

l: war, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 38
s: Mencius says that the Spring and Autumn contains no righteous wars, though one war may be better than another. Correction belongs to supreme authority punishing subjects, while hostile States cannot correct one another; rulers who love benevolence can overcome enemies without relying on warfare.

l: desires, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 38
s: Desires for sweet tastes, beautiful colors, pleasant sounds, fragrant odors, and ease are natural. Mencius teaches that having few desires is best for nourishing the mind, while many desires make it difficult to keep the heart.

l: natural human feelings, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 38
s: Natural human feelings include desires for sensory pleasure and ease, as well as aversion to injuring others and reluctance to commit certain wrongs. When these feelings are fully extended, they produce benevolence and righteousness.

l: the doctrines of the sages, Mencius, Book VII (Jin Xin), Part II / Chapter 1 .. Chapter 38
s: The doctrines of the sages are passed down through successive generations by direct observation and transmission. From Yao and Shun through Tang, king Wen, and Confucius, the text asks whether anyone remains to transmit them further.

l: The Analects of Confucius
s: The Master teaches that learning, friendship, virtue, filial conduct, sincerity, propriety, and self-examination are central to good character and government. The philosopher Yu explains that filial piety and fraternal submission are roots of benevolent actions, while ease in propriety must remain regulated by propriety itself. Tsang, Tsze-hsia, Tsze-kung, and Tsze-ch'in discuss self-examination, conduct toward parents and friends, learning, and the Master’s methods. The unit concludes that people should seek to understand others and correct their own faults rather than be distressed when others do not understand them.

l: The Master, The Analects of Confucius
s: The Master teaches perseverance in learning, delight in friends, filial and respectful conduct, sincerity, love for others, friendship with the good, and correction of faults. He says that a person should be earnest in action, careful in speech, and associate with principled men. He also says that he is troubled not by men's failure to know him but by his own failure to know men.

l: the philosopher Yu, The Analects of Confucius
s: The philosopher Yu says that filial piety and fraternal submission are the root of benevolent actions. He teaches that natural ease in practising propriety is valuable when regulated by the rules of propriety.

l: the superior man, The Analects of Confucius
s: The superior man focuses attention on what is radical, because once the foundation is established, practical courses naturally arise.

l: a man of complete virtue, The Analects of Confucius
s: A man of complete virtue remains undisturbed when men take no note of him. He does not seek to gratify his appetite or comforts, is earnest in action, careful in speech, and keeps company with principled men so that he may be rectified.

l: men, The Analects of Confucius
s: Men may fail to take note of a man of complete virtue or fail to know the Master. The Master says that the greater concern is not knowing men.

l: parents, The Analects of Confucius
s: Parents receive careful funeral rites, followed by ceremonies of sacrifice after they are long gone. A youth should serve his parents by being filial and exerting his utmost strength.

l: learning, The Analects of Confucius
s: Learning is made solid by gravity and begins with perseverance and application. A person who serves parents, prince, and friends well may be considered learned even if men say he has not learned.

l: virtue, The Analects of Confucius
s: Virtue is associated with sincerity, filial and fraternal conduct, and freedom from discomposure. Fine words and an insinuating appearance are seldom associated with true virtue.

l: filial piety, The Analects of Confucius
s: Filial piety is presented as a root of benevolent actions. A youth should show it at home and exert his utmost strength in serving parents.

l: fraternal submission, The Analects of Confucius
s: Fraternal submission is presented with filial piety as a root of benevolent actions. A youth should be respectful to his elders when abroad.

l: propriety, The Analects of Confucius
s: Propriety guides agreements, respect, relationships, conduct toward wealth, and the proper use of natural ease. The rules of propriety must regulate ease rather than be set aside by it.

l: faithfulness and sincerity, The Analects of Confucius
s: Faithfulness and sincerity are to be held as first principles. Sincerity is also required in business, friendship, government, and speech.

l: The Analects of Confucius, Book II (Wei Chang)
s: This unit presents the Master’s teachings on governing through virtue, propriety, and the advancement of the upright. Confucius explains filial piety as obedience to propriety, reverence, care for parents, and proper service in life and death. The unit also describes learning, knowledge, the superior man, truthfulness, and conduct that avoids blame and regret. It concludes that sacrificing to an inappropriate spirit is flattery and that failing to do what is right shows lack of courage.

l: Confucius, The Analects of Confucius, Book II (Wei Chang)
s: Confucius teaches that people submit when the upright are advanced and the crooked are set aside. He also explains that future affairs can be known from how dynasties follow, alter, or add to earlier regulations.

l: people, The Analects of Confucius, Book II (Wei Chang)
s: People led by laws and punishments try to avoid punishment but lack shame. When led by virtue and the rules of propriety, they develop a sense of shame and become good; they also submit to a ruler who advances the upright.

l: superior man, The Analects of Confucius, Book II (Wei Chang)
s: The superior man is described as acting before speaking and speaking according to his actions. He is catholic and not partisan, and the accomplished scholar is said not to be a utensil.

l: government, The Analects of Confucius, Book II (Wei Chang)
s: Government should be exercised through virtue, filial and brotherly duties, gravity, kindness, and the advancement of the good. Confucius says these qualities constitute government even without holding office.

l: virtue, The Analects of Confucius, Book II (Wei Chang)
s: Virtue guides people toward shame and goodness when it is used in governing. A ruler who presides with gravity, acts filially and kindly, and advances the good encourages people to seek virtue.

l: filial piety, The Analects of Confucius, Book II (Wei Chang)
s: Filial piety includes not being disobedient, serving and burying parents according to propriety, sacrificing to them according to propriety, caring about their health, and showing reverence rather than mere support. It also includes filial and brotherly duties that can be displayed in government.

l: rules of propriety, The Analects of Confucius, Book II (Wei Chang)
s: The rules of propriety are used to give people uniformity and lead them toward shame and goodness. They govern how parents are served, buried, and sacrificed to, and how elders are treated.

l: learning, The Analects of Confucius, Book II (Wei Chang)
s: Learning without thought is labour lost, while thought without learning is perilous. A person who cherishes old knowledge while continually acquiring new knowledge may become a teacher of others.

l: knowledge, The Analects of Confucius, Book II (Wei Chang)
s: Knowledge consists in recognizing what one knows and admitting what one does not know. It also involves hearing and seeing much, setting aside doubtful or perilous points, and speaking and acting cautiously.

l: The Analects of Confucius, Book III (Pa Yih)
s: This unit presents Confucius's judgments on propriety, ritual, music, governance, and moral conduct. He criticizes abuses of rank and ceremony, stresses humanity, reverence, sorrow, and proper observance, and discusses how princes and ministers should relate. The unit also records teachings about music, archery, sacrifices, and the traditions of past dynasties. Confucius is portrayed as valuing faithful ritual practice while condemning empty or excessive observance.

l: Confucius, The Analects of Confucius, Book III (Pa Yih)
s: Confucius criticizes the head of the Chi family for displaying eight rows of pantomimes and condemns improper sacrifices, empty ceremony, and abuses of rank. He teaches that humanity should precede rites and music, that ceremonies should be observed with appropriate restraint and reverence, and that a prince should employ ministers according to propriety while ministers serve with faithfulness. He follows Chau's complete and elegant regulations and explains that music should begin in unity, proceed in harmony, and conclude properly.

l: virtues proper to humanity, The Analects of Confucius, Book III (Pa Yih)
s: The virtues proper to humanity are presented as necessary foundations for rites of propriety and music. Without them, a person has no proper relation to either.

l: rites of propriety, The Analects of Confucius, Book III (Pa Yih)
s: Rites of propriety should follow the preparation of the plain ground and should be practiced with restraint, reverence, and sincerity. Their full observance in serving a prince may be mistaken for flattery, while neglecting their proper forms reveals ignorance of propriety.

l: music, The Analects of Confucius, Book III (Pa Yih)
s: Music should express enjoyment without licentiousness and grief without harmful excess. Confucius teaches that its parts should begin together, remain harmonious while distinct, flow without interruption, and reach a proper conclusion.

l: kingdom, The Analects of Confucius, Book III (Pa Yih)
s: The kingdom is described as having long been without the principles of truth and right. Heaven is said to be preparing to use Confucius as a bell with a wooden tongue to restore those principles.

l: prince, The Analects of Confucius, Book III (Pa Yih)
s: A prince should employ ministers according to the rules of propriety. Princes are also associated with proper ceremonial forms, including screens at their gates and stands for inverted cups during friendly meetings.

l: ministers, The Analects of Confucius, Book III (Pa Yih)
s: Ministers should serve their prince with faithfulness. The text also criticizes arrangements in which officers perform double duties, treating them as evidence relevant to questions of propriety and governance.

l: The Analects of Confucius, Book IV (Le Jin)
s: The Master teaches that virtue, proper conduct, and the right way should guide personal life, government, relationships, and responses to hardship. He explains that the superior man follows righteousness, values virtue over comfort or gain, and remains committed to it in haste and danger. The text also describes duties of a son toward parents and warns against excessive remonstrance in service and friendship. Tsang identifies the Master's doctrine of an all-pervading unity as being true to one's nature and benevolently exercising it toward others.

l: The Master, The Analects of Confucius, Book IV (Le Jin)
s: The Master teaches that virtue should govern a person's choices, relationships, conduct, and response to poverty, danger, and advantage. He urges people to seek the right way, examine themselves, honor parents, and make their actions accord with their words.

l: virtue, The Analects of Confucius, Book IV (Le Jin)
s: Virtue is presented as the basis of an excellent neighborhood and as the condition for rightly loving or hating others. The virtuous rest in virtue, cleave to it in hardship and danger, and gain neighbors through practicing it.

l: superior man, The Analects of Confucius, Book IV (Le Jin)
s: The superior man follows what is right rather than taking a fixed position for or against things. He thinks of virtue, righteousness, and the sanctions of law, avoids acting contrary to virtue, and is slow in speech but earnest in conduct.

l: son, The Analects of Confucius, Book IV (Le Jin)
s: The son may gently remonstrate with parents, but continues to show reverence when they do not accept his advice and does not murmur if punished. While parents are alive, he should not travel far without a fixed destination, and if he preserves his father's way for three years, he may be called filial.

l: parents, The Analects of Confucius, Book IV (Le Jin)
s: Parents' ages should be kept in the son's memory as a source both of joy and fear. A son's service to them includes gentle remonstrance, increased reverence, and continued purpose even when they reject his advice.

l: the right way, The Analects of Confucius, Book IV (Le Jin)
s: The right way is something a person may hear in the morning and then face death without regret. A person who learns it should value it above concern for recognition or worldly position.

l: righteousness, The Analects of Confucius, Book IV (Le Jin)
s: Righteousness occupies the mind of the superior man, while the mean man is concerned with gain. The superior man follows what is right rather than setting his mind for or against anything.

l: doctrine of an all-pervading unity, The Analects of Confucius, Book IV (Le Jin)
s: The Master describes his doctrine as an all-pervading unity. Tsang explains it as being true to the principles of one's nature and exercising them benevolently toward others.

l: The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: This document is a sequence of sayings and judgments by the Master about character, learning, conduct, and fitness for public life. It begins with his confidence in Kung-ye Ch'ang and Nan Yung, expressed through marriages into his family, and praises Tsze-chien’s virtue as connected with virtuous men in Lu. The Master assesses several disciples: Tsze-kung is a gemmed sacrificial utensil but inferior to Hui in understanding; Tsze-lu, Ch'iu, and Ch'ih have evident abilities yet are not confirmed as perfectly virtuous; Ch'i-tiao K'ai pleases him by declining office until ready. He criticizes empty eloquence, impulsiveness, daytime sleep, passion, and unsupported claims of moral achievement, while valuing conduct over words. The sayings also evaluate public figures and exemplary behavior. Kung-wan is honored for learning from inferiors; Tsze-ch'an is humble, respectful, kind, and just; Yen P'ing sustains respect in friendship; and Tsze-wan and Ch'an Wan are called loyal and pure without being declared perfectly virtuous. The Master questions Tsang Wan’s ornamented tortoise house and Wei-shang Kao’s uprightness, praises Po-i and Shu-ch'i for not retaining former wrongs, and rejects flattering speech, affected respect, and concealed resentment. Amid concern that his doctrines make no way, the Master imagines leaving by sea, calls for a return from Ch'an, and urges his ambitious pupils to learn restraint and form. The document closes with wishes voiced by Chi Lu, Yen Yuan, and the Master: generosity, modesty, rest for the aged, sincerity toward friends, and tenderness toward the young. It ends with the Master’s disappointment at people’s failure to recognize their own faults, alongside his insistence that love of learning distinguishes him even from honourable and sincere people.

l: Kung-ye Ch'ang, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: Kung-ye Ch'ang, unjustly put in bonds, was considered suitable for marriage by The Master and received The Master’s daughter as wife.

l: The Master, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: The Master is a teacher and judge of character whose doctrines are not making their way. He speaks favorably of Kung-ye Ch'ang and Nan Yung, giving his own daughter to the former and his elder brother's daughter to the latter. He praises superior virtue, recognizes ability in several people, and assigns likely roles to Tsze-lu, Ch'iu, and Ch'ih, yet repeatedly refuses to call people perfectly virtuous when he does not know that they meet that standard. He values learning, sincerity, loyalty, purity, firmness, self-knowledge, and conduct that bears out words. After Tsai Yu sleeps in daytime, he explains that he has changed from crediting men's words to looking at their conduct. He criticizes readiness of tongue, fine words, insinuating appearance, excessive respect, false friendliness, elaborate display, passion mistaken for firmness, and failure to perceive one's own faults. In Ch'an, he longs to return and reflects critically on his school. His own wish is to give rest to the aged, show sincerity to friends, and treat the young tenderly. He ends by saying that even a small hamlet may contain someone as honourable and sincere as he is, though none more fond of learning.

l: Nan Yung, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: Nan Yung is praised by The Master as fit to remain in office under good government and able to avoid punishment and disgrace under bad government; The Master gives him his elder brother’s daughter as wife.

l: Tsze-chien, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: Tsze-chien is a man described by The Master as of superior virtue, whose character was acquired through virtuous men in Lu.

l: Lu, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: Lu is presented as a place where virtuous men exist. Their presence is implied to have helped Tsze-chien acquire his character.

l: virtuous men in Lu, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: Virtuous men in Lu exist there and enable Tsze-chien’s acquisition of character.

l: superior virtue, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: Superior virtue is the quality The Master attributes to Tsze-chien. Yung is described as truly virtuous, though the Master says he does not know whether this is so.

l: Tsze-kung, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: Tsze-kung is described as a utensil, specifically a gemmed sacrificial utensil. He asks the Master for an assessment of himself and what kind of utensil he is. He refuses comparison with Hui, saying Hui grasps a whole subject from one point while he reaches only a second. He states a wish for reciprocal restraint toward others, but the Master says he has not attained it. He says some of the Master's teachings can be heard while discourses on man's nature and Heaven cannot, and he asks why Kung-wan received the title Wan.

l: utensil, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: The Master describes Tsze-kung as a utensil.

s: is_a utensil [sacrificial] The Master identifies Tsze-kung as a gemmed sacrificial utensil.

l: Yung, The Analects of Confucius, Book V (Kung-Ye Ch'Ang)
s: Yung is said to be truly virtuous but not ready with his tongue; the Master says he does not know whether Yung is truly virtuous.
